claims.text: A defect-aware predictive model will significantly improve electronic or thermal conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr in both the near-0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The initial material is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr produced using vacuum sintering.
The nominal microstructure contains a beta-BCC phase.
The specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen produces interstitial solid-solution strengthening and local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed methodology will represent oxygen interstitials, lattice distortions, and temperature-dependent scattering mechanisms.
Low-temperature scattering and possible quantum effects become important in the near-0–200 K regime.
Phonon, defect, and interstitial-induced scattering dominate transport in the 300–1200 K regime.
Interstitial oxygen introduces defect-scattering centers and local distortions that modify electronic and phonon transport pathways.
Representing oxygen-induced defects, defect energetics, and disorder will bridge the gap between ideal-crystal predictions and the behavior of sintered samples.
Oxygen-induced disorder alters temperature-dependent carrier scattering and conductivity.
The defect-aware model will predict lower thermal or electrical conductivity than perfect-crystal models.
In the 300–1200 K regime, oxygen-defect scattering will reduce conductivity by a measurable margin.
In the 0–200 K regime, quantum effects and defect scattering will produce a conductivity plateau or altered activation behavior.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical models systematically overestimate conductivity for HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical models fail to capture defect-related conductivity modifications in oxygen-containing specimens.
The proposed improvement is limited to bulk sintered samples with defect chemistry near 1 wt.% oxygen and temperatures from near 0 K to about 1200 K.
The model may not apply to substantially different oxygen contents or synthesis routes.
A greater-than-20% statistically significant deviation from perfect-crystal predictions is proposed as the benchmark for a defect-induced effect.
Failure of oxygen-containing measurements to deviate from perfect-crystal predictions or to exhibit the predicted defect-induced trends would falsify the claimed accuracy improvement.
